sections.title: Overview
sections.content: NC State describes Tradescantia as a trailing, fast-growing genus readily propagated by stem cuttings. This genus-level description is not a substitute for a species account of T. zebrina.

sections.title: Identification
sections.content: Tradescantia zebrina is a trailing plant with alternating green and silver stripes and purple undersides; the linked NC State account is genus-level, so compare the plant itself with a species-specific reference before treating this as confirmed.

sections.title: Light
sections.content: Bright indirect light is a safe starting point; acclimate gradually before giving direct sun.

sections.title: Watering
sections.content: Water thoroughly when the upper mix begins to dry, then drain the saucer. Adjust for heat and pot size.

sections.title: Soil and drainage
sections.content: Use porous indoor potting mix and a container with drainage; avoid dense garden soil.

sections.title: Temperature
sections.content: Keep in a warm, stable spot away from cold drafts and air-conditioning vents.

sections.title: Humidity
sections.content: Average indoor humidity is usually workable; improve airflow if foliage stays wet or leaf edges dry.

sections.title: Fertilizing
sections.content: Use dilute balanced houseplant fertilizer during active growth; reduce or pause in slow periods.

sections.title: Pruning
sections.content: Pinch leggy stems and remove yellow leaves with clean tools; avoid heavy pruning at once.

sections.title: Propagation
sections.content: Stem cuttings or division may work depending on the species; use clean tools and airy, lightly moist medium.

sections.title: Toxicity and safety
sections.content: A species-specific toxicity assessment is not included here. As a precaution, do not eat any part or use it medicinally; keep it away from children and pets until its safety is checked. If ingestion occurs, contact a local poison service or clinician.

sections.title: Common problems
sections.content: Inspect for mites, scale and mealybugs; yellowing can follow excess water or poor drainage.

sections.title: Seasonal care
sections.content: In Dhaka, protect from midday sun and monsoon saturation; adjust watering to pot dryness and slower cool-season growth.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Syngonium podophyllum is a tropical shrub that becomes a climbing vine with age. NC State describes juvenile arrow-shaped foliage and mature leaves that become lobed or divided.

sections.title: Identification
sections.content: Juvenile Syngonium podophyllum leaves are arrow-shaped; mature leaves become lobed and may divide into several segments. Leaf shape changes with maturity, so assess age before judging identity.

sections.title: Light
sections.content: Provide bright shade or partial shade. NC State cautions that full sun can burn or bleach Syngonium podophyllum foliage.

sections.title: Watering
sections.content: Keep the Syngonium podophyllum growing medium moist; avoid leaving the roots saturated. The source does not give a fixed watering interval.

sections.title: Soil and drainage
sections.content: Use porous indoor potting mix and a container with drainage; avoid dense garden soil.

sections.title: Temperature
sections.content: Keep in a warm, stable spot away from cold drafts and air-conditioning vents.

sections.title: Humidity
sections.content: NC State recommends a warm, humid setting for Syngonium podophyllum. Provide airflow and avoid stagnant, persistently wet foliage.

sections.title: Fertilizing
sections.content: Use dilute balanced houseplant fertilizer during active growth; reduce or pause in slow periods.

sections.title: Pruning
sections.content: To keep juvenile arrowhead foliage and a bushier habit, cut stems back as they begin to climb. NC State also notes that trimming roots during occasional repotting can help manage size.

sections.title: Propagation
sections.content: NC State lists division, layering and stem cuttings for Syngonium podophyllum.

sections.title: Toxicity and safety
sections.content: Syngonium podophyllum contains calcium oxalate crystals. NC State reports oral irritation and swelling, drooling, vomiting and difficulty swallowing after exposure; keep away from children and pets and avoid sap contact.

sections.title: Common problems
sections.content: NC State reports aphids, mealybugs and spider mites, plus bacterial leaf spots and soft rot, on Syngonium podophyllum. Check for the cause before treatment.

sections.title: Seasonal care
sections.content: In Dhaka, protect from midday sun and monsoon saturation; adjust watering to pot dryness and slower cool-season growth.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Nephrolepis exaltata is a tropical/subtropical terrestrial or epiphytic fern grown as the Boston fern houseplant. It produces arching fronds and spores on the undersides.

sections.title: Identification
sections.content: Nephrolepis exaltata is a Boston fern with divided fronds bearing rows of leaflets; spores form on the undersides of mature fronds. The ASPCA toxicity entry is specifically for the Boston fern form.

sections.title: Light
sections.content: Give Boston fern bright, indirect light.

sections.title: Watering
sections.content: Keep Boston fern soil moist and do not let it dry out completely. Reduce watering in winter when growth slows, while avoiding waterlogged roots.

sections.title: Soil and drainage
sections.content: Use humus-rich, moisture-retentive but freely draining mix; epiphytic types need an airy medium.

sections.title: Temperature
sections.content: NC State gives 60–70°F (about 16–21°C) as a suitable warm indoor range for Nephrolepis exaltata.

sections.title: Humidity
sections.content: Boston fern needs high humidity. A humid room or pebble tray can help; allow air movement around the fronds.

sections.title: Fertilizing
sections.content: Feed lightly with dilute balanced fertilizer during active growth; reduce when growth slows.

sections.title: Pruning
sections.content: Remove dead or badly damaged fronds at the base; keep healthy fronds.

sections.title: Propagation
sections.content: Divide established clumps or rhizomes during active growth; keep divisions humid and evenly moist.

sections.title: Toxicity and safety
sections.content: A species-specific toxicity assessment is not included here. As a precaution, do not eat any part or use it medicinally; keep it away from children and pets until its safety is checked. If ingestion occurs, contact a local poison service or clinician.

sections.title: Common problems
sections.content: Watch for dry frond tips, scale and spider mites; check moisture and airflow before treatment.

sections.title: Seasonal care
sections.content: In Dhaka’s hot dry season check pots more often and shade from harsh afternoon sun; water less during cool slow growth.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Asplenium nidus is a tropical evergreen epiphytic fern. Its upright, strap-shaped fronds form a funnel-shaped rosette that catches leaf litter.

sections.title: Identification
sections.content: Look for broad, simple, strap-shaped fronds with wavy margins and a dark midrib, arranged in a central funnel-shaped rosette. Asplenium nidus reproduces by spores rather than flowers or fruit.

sections.title: Light
sections.content: Bright indirect light or light shade suits Asplenium nidus; excess sun may yellow the fronds or slow growth.

sections.title: Watering
sections.content: Keep the porous fern medium moist and do not allow Asplenium nidus to dry out. Use an open mix so moisture does not become waterlogging.

sections.title: Soil and drainage
sections.content: Use a rich, moist, porous fern mix for this epiphyte.

sections.title: Temperature
sections.content: NC State says Asplenium nidus will not survive below 40°F (about 4°C); its ideal temperature range is 60–70°F (about 16–21°C).

sections.title: Humidity
sections.content: This rainforest fern does not tolerate dry conditions; provide high humidity while avoiding stagnant air.

sections.title: Fertilizing
sections.content: NC State notes that active growth may benefit from a monthly application of dilute liquid fertilizer. Use a conservative dilution and reduce feeding when growth slows.

sections.title: Pruning
sections.content: Remove dead or badly damaged fronds at the base; keep healthy fronds.

sections.title: Propagation
sections.content: Divide established clumps or rhizomes during active growth; keep divisions humid and evenly moist.

sections.content: A species-specific toxicity assessment is not included here. As a precaution, do not eat any part or use it medicinally; keep it away from children and pets until its safety is checked. If ingestion occurs, contact a local poison service or clinician.

sections.title: Common problems
sections.content: Asplenium nidus is susceptible to slugs, snails, scale, mealybugs, bacterial leaf diseases and leaf nematodes. NC State cautions that the fronds are fragile and sensitive to chemical insecticides.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Phlebodium aureum is a rhizomatous epiphytic fern from the American tropics. Its creeping golden-scaled rhizomes and deeply lobed blue-green fronds distinguish it from true palms despite the common name cabbage palm fern.

sections.title: Identification
sections.content: Identify Phlebodium aureum by its creeping, golden-scaled rhizomes and large, deeply lobed fronds; round sori occur in rows on either side of the pinna midrib.

sections.title: Light
sections.content: Provide partial shade or dappled light for Phlebodium aureum.

sections.title: Watering
sections.content: Use a moist but not soggy substrate. Phlebodium aureum tolerates some drying between waterings.

sections.title: Soil and drainage
sections.content: Use a loose, organic, acidic medium with good drainage for this epiphytic fern.

sections.title: Temperature

sections.title: Humidity
sections.content: Medium to high humidity and good air circulation suit Phlebodium aureum. Frond browning can indicate low humidity; curling can signal low humidity or underwatering.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Platycerium bifurcatum is an epiphytic staghorn fern that grows on support rather than parasitizing a host. It forms sterile shield fronds and branching fertile fronds.

sections.title: Soil and drainage

sections.content: Dypsis lutescens (areca/butterfly palm) is a clumping tropical palm. UF/IFAS describes it as suited to warm climates and fertile, acidic, well-drained soil; indoors it needs bright filtered light and steady moisture without standing water.

sections.title: Identification
sections.content: A clump of slender yellow-green canes with arching feather-shaped fronds is characteristic of Dypsis lutescens. Frond and cane color vary with light and age.

sections.content: Beaucarnea recurvata is an evergreen, drought-tolerant succulent tree native to Mexico. The swollen caudex stores water; the common name ponytail palm is misleading because it is not a true palm.

sections.content: Provide a sunny window for Beaucarnea recurvata; acclimate gradually before moving it to a protected patio.

sections.title: Soil and drainage

sections.content: NC State describes Beaucarnea recurvata as hardy to about 50°F (10°C); bring container plants into protection before colder conditions.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Adenium obesum is a drought-tolerant succulent shrub with a swollen caudex, native to Africa and the Arabian Peninsula. NC State reports a slow growth rate and summer flowering.

sections.title: Identification
sections.content: Adenium obesum has a thick gray-green caudex, glossy leaves near branch tips, showy five-lobed flowers and paired pod-like follicles. Flower colours and forms vary among cultivars.

sections.title: Light
sections.content: Grow Adenium obesum in full sun; acclimate a sheltered container plant gradually when moving it outdoors.

sections.title: Watering
sections.content: Let the succulent growing medium dry between waterings. Water during active growth; reduce watering during dormancy. Excessively wet soil can cause rot.

sections.title: Soil and drainage
sections.content: Use a cactus/succulent medium and a pot with multiple drainage holes. NC State specifies good drainage for Adenium obesum.

sections.title: Temperature
sections.content: Protect from chilling, especially when the pot is wet; maintain warmth during active growth.

sections.title: Humidity
sections.content: Ordinary room humidity is adequate; prioritize airflow and fast drainage over misting.

sections.title: Fertilizing
sections.content: Feed sparingly with diluted balanced fertilizer in active growth; skip dormant or stressed plants.

sections.title: Pruning
sections.content: Prune only damaged or overlong growth; allow cuts to dry before watering.

sections.title: Propagation
sections.content: NC State lists seed, stem cuttings and grafting for Adenium obesum; success and retention of cultivar traits vary by method.

sections.title: Toxicity and safety
sections.content: NC State reports cardiac glycosides and poisonous plant parts throughout Adenium obesum; ingestion can cause gastrointestinal and cardiac effects, and milky sap may cause contact dermatitis. Wear gloves when pruning and keep the plant away from children and pets.

sections.title: Common problems

sections.title: Seasonal care

sections.content: Use fertile, well-drained soil and keep the bulb crown from sitting in persistent water.

sections.title: Temperature
sections.content: Keep warm in active growth; reduce watering if foliage naturally becomes dormant.

sections.title: Humidity
sections.content: No special humidity treatment; keep bulbs ventilated and crowns free of trapped moisture.

sections.title: Fertilizing
sections.content: Feed lightly while leaves are growing; let foliage yellow naturally after bloom.

sections.title: Pruning
sections.content: Remove faded flowers if desired, but retain green foliage until it yellows.

sections.title: Propagation
sections.content: Separate offsets or divide clumps; retain roots and avoid damage to the basal plate.

sections.title: Toxicity and safety
sections.content: Treat the bulb as potentially toxic: NC State reports low-severity ingestion poisoning for Hymenocallis, with nausea, vomiting and diarrhea associated with lycorine and related alkaloids. This is genus-level evidence, not a species-specific toxicology study.

sections.title: Common problems
sections.content: Check for bulb rot in wet soil and inspect leaves for slugs or chewing pests.

sections.title: Seasonal care
sections.content: Let leaves finish naturally after bloom; maintain free drainage during Dhaka’s rainy season.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Impatiens balsamina is a frost-tender, fast-growing annual with succulent stems and cup-shaped flowers. It prefers moist conditions and readily self-seeds.

sections.title: Identification
sections.content: Garden balsam has succulent upright stems, serrated lance-shaped leaves and cup-shaped flowers; mature seed pods burst when touched.

sections.title: Light

sections.title: Soil and drainage

sections.title: Temperature
sections.content: Keep warm and shelter from cold drafts; growth slows in cool weather.

sections.content: Use balanced flowering-plant fertilizer at label rate during active growth.

sections.title: Pruning

sections.title: Propagation
sections.content: Use seed or soft cuttings depending on species; keep warm and lightly moist while establishing.

sections.title: Toxicity and safety
